planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Požegača is self-fertile but benefits from another European plum nearby for heavier cropping.

directions: Požegača is the classic old Serbian and wider Balkan plum, grown for centuries in the Šumadija and western Serbian hill country as the backbone of the region's rakija and šljivovica distilling tradition as well as for sun-dried prunes. The small, deep blue-purple, freestone fruit has dense, very sweet flesh with high sugar content that concentrates well on drying, and the tree is a dependable, long-lived small standard that tolerates poorer hillside soils better than many modern plum selections. It ripens in late summer and is harvested over a staggered window as fruit drops, a trait that suits traditional orchard gathering rather than a single clean pick. Several newer commercial Balkan plums, including the Čačak-bred cultivars, were developed in part to improve on Požegača's disease susceptibility while keeping its rich, distilling-grade sweetness.

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in early spring in full sun; it is partially self-fertile but sets a heavier, more even crop with another European plum blooming nearby.

directions: Čačanska Lepotica (the name translates roughly as 'beauty of Čačak') was bred at the Fruit Research Institute in Čačak, Serbia, in the mid-twentieth century and has since become one of the most widely planted dessert plums across the Balkans and much of Eastern Europe. It bears large, oval, reddish-purple fruit with firm, juicy, sweet yellow flesh that separates cleanly from the pit, ripening in mid-to-late summer ahead of the related Čačanska Rodna. The tree begins bearing young and crops heavily and reliably, making it a popular dooryard choice as well as a commercial variety for fresh eating. Fruit is excellent eaten fresh off the tree but also holds up well for jam, compote, and the region's plum brandy traditions.

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed in early fall so plants establish before hard frost; Sangaste overwinters as a low rosette and resumes rapid growth, bolting and heading the following summer.

directions: Sangaste rye was bred in the 1870s-1890s by Friedrich Georg Magnus von Berg at Sangaste Manor in southern Estonia, selected over generations for exceptionally tall, thick stems and unusually large grain heads, and it went on to win a gold medal at the 1900 Paris World Exhibition as one of the finest rye landraces in Europe. It is still maintained today as a living heritage grain by Estonian plant breeding institutions and small-scale growers who value both its history and its flavorful, dark, old-style rye bread flour. Grow it on lean, sandy soil with modest fertility, since rich garden soil pushes the already-tall stems into lodging; a fall sowing lets it vernalize over winter and head out the following summer, after which the long straw was traditionally also valued for thatching.

common_name: Berner Rose Potato (Swiss Heirloom Pink-Skinned Potato)

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces, each with 2-3 eyes, 4 inches deep in cool, fertile soil; hill soil around the stems as they grow to protect developing tubers from light.

directions: Berner Rose is an old Swiss heirloom potato from the canton of Bern, with distinctive pink-red skin and pale yellow, waxy-to-floury flesh that holds its shape well when cooked. It was long grown in Swiss mountain kitchen gardens and has been preserved and distributed in recent decades by Swiss heritage seed organizations working to keep regional potato landraces in circulation. The medium-late maturing tubers store well into winter and are especially prized in Switzerland for rösti and for simple boiled or roasted preparations where the potato's firm texture and nutty flavor stand on their own. Give it full sun, consistent moisture during tuber set, and well-drained soil, since standing water promotes rot in the thin-skinned tubers.

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in early spring in full sun with sharp drainage and, if possible, a sheltered site away from low frost pockets since apricots bloom very early and are vulnerable to spring frost.

directions: Luizet was selected in Isère, France in the nineteenth century but became the defining apricot variety of the Valais region of Switzerland, where entire hillsides above the Rhone valley were planted to it and it remains the traditional base for Valais apricot preserves and the apricot brandy known locally as Abricotine. The medium-to-large fruit has orange-yellow skin with a light red blush and sweet, aromatic, slightly firm orange flesh that is well suited to fresh eating, drying, jam, and distilling. The tree is reliably self-fertile and productive but, like most apricots, flowers early and benefits from a site with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to the blossoms. Harvest when fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and separates easily from the stem for the best balance of sugar and aromatic flavor.

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and site a compatible pollinizer nearby since Aport is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Aport is a historic apple long cultivated in the orchards around Almaty, Kazakhstan, a region that sits within the native range of the wild apple Malus sieversii, widely regarded as a major wild ancestor of the domesticated apple. The fruit is notably large, often exceeding a pound, with a thin red-striped skin over dense, aromatic, juicy white flesh with a balanced sweet-tart flavor that made it famous in Russian and Central Asian markets through the Soviet era. Trees are vigorous and need generous spacing and a sturdy support system when young, since limbs can bend under the weight of the oversized fruit. Harvest in early autumn once fruit develops full color and fragrance; the apples are prized fresh but also hold up well for juicing and preserving given their dense flesh.
